title: Jason Cohen on bootstrapping's hard truths: judging advice, filtering tradeoffs, and finding your role
summary: Jason Cohen talks with Justin Jackson about why most startup advice is survivorship-biased and tied to the giver's goals. He covers how to decide among incomparable options with filters, the real time cost of bootstrapping, why "struggle porn" is a symptom, and a like/good-at/company-needs framework for deciding your role.

principles.text: Most advice is the giver advising themselves. Weigh whether their goals and context match yours before acting on it.
principles.quote: when people give advice what they really are doing is giving themselves advice

principles.text: Beware survivor bias: a practice shared by winners proves little unless failures didn't do the same thing.
principles.quote: the problem is that five years later forty percent of those companies were bankrupt

principles.text: When equally plausible strategies conflict, pick the one that excites you; your extra energy and time tips the odds.
principles.quote: why not pick the one that you're personally really jazzed about because whatever you're jazzed about you're going automatically to put in that extra energy in that time

principles.text: Trade-offs across incomparable dimensions can't be stack-ranked. Set hard limits as filters, then optimize one or two dimensions.
principles.quote: you can decide there are certain limits or certain thresholds I will not cross

principles.text: Bootstrapping takes far more than a few hours a week. Admit the real time cost; struggle means the business isn't working yet.
principles.quote: you take something like 40 hours a week of work for something like two years to get the damn thing off the ground

principles.text: Choose your role by what you like, what you're good at, and what the company needs. Founders miss the 'company needs' leg because nobody tells them.
principles.quote: what do I like what am I good at what does the company need yeah those are the three things
